opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a very real concern, and it's one we hear constantly from enterprise customers. When you send a prompt to a hosted API, you're sending your data outside your four walls. The providers have gotten much better about this. They offer contractual guarantees that they won't train on your data, retention windows, enterprise tiers, and so on. Frankly, I think the big labs have strong incentives to honor those commitments, because their business depends on trust.

But for a lot of companies, a contractual promise isn't the same as control. If you're a bank, a healthcare provider, a defense contractor, or just a company whose crown jewels are its proprietary data and code, the question isn't only "will they misuse it?" It's also "where does it physically sit, who can be compelled to hand it over, what happens in a breach, and can I prove to my regulators where it went?" Those are hard questions to answer when the data is leaving your environment.

So what we're seeing is a bifurcation. For experimentation, prototyping, and less sensitive workloads, people happily use the APIs. They're convenient and the models are excellent. But as AI moves into production and touches core business data, more enterprises want to run inference themselves, either on-prem or in a private cloud, using open-weight models that are now very capable, or licensed models deployed inside their own environment.

That shift is a big part of why inference infrastructure matters so much. If enterprises are going to run these models themselves, they need hardware that delivers that capability efficiently. They need low latency, good throughput, and reasonable power and cost, without having to build a hyperscaler-sized data center. That's exactly the problem we're focused on at d-Matrix.

So my assessment is that the concern is legitimate. It's not paranoia, it's governance. And the answer for many companies won't be "trust the API more." It will be "bring the model to the data instead of sending the data to the model."

r001.rationale: The candidate mentions provider promises not to train on submitted data and retention windows, but does not identify zero-data-retention guarantees or attribute them specifically to OpenAI or Anthropic.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not compare AI API providers’ data access with Microsoft 365’s access to company information.

fable-5.1.text:
Look, I think the concern is legitimate, but I'd separate it into two different questions, because people tend to conflate them.

The first question is contractual and policy: does the provider train on your data, who can see it, where does it live? And honestly, the big labs have mostly answered that for enterprise customers. If you're on an enterprise agreement with OpenAI or Anthropic, your prompts aren't used for training, there's zero or limited retention, there's SOC 2, all of that. For a lot of companies, that's sufficient. They trust their cloud provider with their data already, and this isn't fundamentally different.

The second question is architectural, and this is the one I spend more time thinking about. The moment you make an API call to a frontier model, your data has to leave your perimeter. It has to be in the clear, at some point, on somebody else's hardware, because the model has to read it to do anything useful. You can encrypt it in transit, you can encrypt it at rest, but at inference time it's exposed. So no matter how good the contract is, you're relying on trust rather than on physics.

And for certain categories of data, trust isn't enough. If you're a bank, a defense contractor, a hospital, a law firm, you have regulatory or fiduciary reasons why "we have a good contract" isn't an acceptable answer. Those customers want the model to come to the data, not the data to go to the model.

So what we're seeing, and this is a big part of why I'm bullish on inference moving to the edge and into enterprise data centers, is a bifurcation. The frontier models through an API for general-purpose work where the data isn't that sensitive. And then open or fine-tuned models running on infrastructure the company controls for anything proprietary. The open models are now good enough that that second path is actually viable, which wasn't true two years ago.

The last thing I'd say is that the concern isn't really about OpenAI or Anthropic being bad actors. I don't think they are. It's that concentration risk is real. If every company's proprietary knowledge flows through two or three providers, that's a lot of eggs in a very small basket, and I think sophisticated buyers are starting to price that in.

r001.rationale: The response says enterprise agreements with OpenAI or Anthropic provide zero or limited retention, presenting this as part of how the providers address the concern.

r002.rationale: It compares AI providers with trusted cloud providers in general, but does not mention or specifically compare access with Microsoft 365.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a legitimate concern. If you’re an enterprise, your proprietary data is often what differentiates you. So you need to understand exactly what happens when you send that data to a model provider: where it’s processed, whether it’s retained, who can access it, and whether it can be used for training. Those are separate questions, and using an API doesn’t automatically mean your data is being used to train a model.

For some companies, contractual protections and security controls will be sufficient. For others, particularly when the data is highly sensitive, they’ll want to run the model within an environment they control. That’s why having a choice of models and deployment options matters. You want to bring AI to your proprietary data without giving up control over it.

r001.rationale: The response discusses retention and training as questions to investigate, but does not identify zero-data-retention guarantees by OpenAI or Anthropic as their answer.

r002.rationale: The response does not compare AI providers’ access to proprietary data with Microsoft 365’s access to company information.

For some companies, those protections will be sufficient. For others, particularly with highly sensitive data, the requirement is going to be to run the model within their own environment.
